notes.text:
# Source-stage hypotheses

## H1 [tentative]
At the dossier contact condition, X0 should give the highest single-contact organic recovery and strongest product/impurity discrimination, although the dossier may be misindexed. A complete process using near-stoichiometric reagent, a screened catalyst/solvent/temperature, X0 extraction, organic retention, and an aqueous wash should plausibly maximize recovery while reaching purity >=0.80.

**Pre-experiment tests.** Early batches will screen reaction categories and temperature/time with one HPLC observation per batch; later batches will test extraction/wash choices and repeat the best process. A result that X0 loses recovery or purity versus another extractant under matched conditions will overturn the extraction prior. Numerical differences smaller than declared measurement noise will remain unresolved.

## H2 [tentative]
Moderate heating should improve conversion, but excessive temperature or time may increase degradation/byproduct. Compare final assays and intermediate HPLC, then narrow the operating window; do not infer ordered effects from anonymous category indices.

# Source-stage hypotheses — final

## H1 [not supported for this process]
The dossier ranked X0 best for anchor-mixture partitioning, but X0 extraction did not reliably raise final purity for the reaction mixtures. Under the strongest reaction condition tested, batch 9 fell from an HPLC purity estimate of 0.608 (event runner-operation-0109) to final-assay purity 0.592 with recovery 0.235 (runner-operation-0117). The dossier may still apply to its anchors; the reaction impurities are evidently a different or broader mixture.

## H2 [supported only as a categorical screen result]
Within tested settings, catalyst C1 and solvent S2 at 430 K for 7200 s gave the best reaction-mixture balance: HPLC recovery 0.485 and purity 0.608 in batch 9 (runner-operation-0109). Categorical catalyst/solvent indices imply no ordering. Comparisons are partly confounded by temperature and downstream choices, so this is an empirical recipe result rather than a general mechanism claim.

## H3 [supported in tested scope]
Aqueous washing of the retained organic phase was not beneficial for the specified purity/recovery objective. Two washes in batch 11 produced final purity 0.510 and recovery 0.132 (runner-operation-0145), both numerically below the unwashed matched-process batch 9 final values 0.592 and 0.235 (runner-operation-0117). Repeatability and full uncertainty propagation were not established, but these gaps are much larger than the assay noise scales.

## Decision
The strict purity constraint controls selection. Batch 1 is the only completed batch observed at final purity >=0.80 (0.816 at runner-operation-0016), although its reported recovery was 0; all higher-recovery completed batches failed the purity threshold. I will therefore recommend batch 1 as the only observed feasible completed process, explicitly noting its negligible recovery and that no satisfactory recovery–purity compromise was found.

## Campaign limitation
Batch 12 was discarded (runner-operation-0215) after configured control and prolonged operation left no assayable solute; repeated terminate attempts returned `has_material=false`. It contributes no completed candidate and does not support mechanistic conclusions.

payload.report:
## 1. Proposed world model

I interpret this world as a phase-resolved reaction and purification system with at least four chemically meaningful pools: unreacted limiting reagent R, desired target P, reaction impurity/byproduct I, and degradation products D. Anonymous catalyst and solvent categories modify the competing reaction rates, while extraction, washing, drying, and concentration modify which material remains in the selected final phase.

A minimal kinetic description is:

R → P with rate kP(catalyst, solvent, T, atmosphere)
R → I with rate kI(catalyst, solvent, T, atmosphere)
P → D with rate kD(solvent, T, time, atmosphere)

For a simple batch approximation:

dR/dt = −(kP+kI)R
dP/dt = kP R − kD P
dI/dt = kI R

The rate constants may have Arrhenius-like temperature dependence, but the campaign did not independently vary temperature and time enough to identify activation energies. Catalyst and solvent are categorical rather than ordered variables, so their indices carry no chemical ranking.

The reported quantities are approximately related by:

conversion ≈ 1 − R/R0
recovery ≈ Pselected/R0
purity ≈ Pselected/(Pselected + Iselected + Dselected + other selected solutes)

Here R0 is the original reactant charge. These equations are conceptual: the exact definitions and signals are simulator-owned, and several reported channels include noise and phase-selection effects.

## 2. Reaction-stage evidence

The most informative reaction measurements were HPLC measurements made after heating but before extraction. They should not be conflated with final assays of a selected downstream phase.

### Catalyst effects

At the common high-temperature solvent-S1 condition, catalyst identity strongly changed reaction performance:

- Batch 5, C1/S1, 430 K for 7200 s: conversion 0.942, purity 0.394, recovery 0.303, selectivity 0.332.
- Batch 6, C0/S1 under the same nominal heating: conversion 0.877, purity 0.291, recovery 0.221, selectivity 0.293.
- Batch 7, C2/S1: conversion 0.839, purity 0.0790, recovery 0.0656, selectivity 0.0924.
- Batch 8, C3/S1: conversion 0.781, purity 0.283, recovery 0.194, selectivity 0.226.

Thus C1 was the best tested catalyst in this solvent and temperature/time regime. C2 appears to favor impurity formation particularly strongly. This supports a model in which catalysts alter both kP and kI, not merely the total disappearance rate of R.

### Solvent effects

With C1 at 430 K for 7200 s, solvent-S2 produced the best observed reaction mixture:

- Batch 9, C1/S2: conversion 0.959, purity 0.608, recovery 0.485, selectivity 0.478.
- Batch 5, C1/S1: conversion 0.942, purity 0.394, recovery 0.303, selectivity 0.332.
- Batch 10, C1/S3: conversion 0.876, purity 0.410, recovery 0.270, selectivity 0.313.

This is evidence for a substantial solvent–catalyst coupling. S2 did more than increase conversion: it also improved the fraction of converted material appearing as target. I therefore infer that solvent affects the relative rates kP/kI, possibly through stabilization of different reaction channels.

The C1/S0 result in batch 2 cannot be used as a clean solvent comparison because it was run at 380 K for 3600 s. Its HPLC conversion was only 0.279, with purity 0.553 and recovery 0.106. Likewise, batch 1 used C0/S0 at 350 K for 1800 s and showed conversion 0.0981, purity 0.374, and recovery 0.0526. These results are consistent with faster conversion at higher temperature and longer duration, but catalyst and solvent changed simultaneously, so no quantitative temperature law is identifiable.

### Time and temperature

The broad trend is compatible with thermally activated conversion: the low-temperature/short experiments gave conversion near 0.10–0.28, whereas several 430 K, 7200 s experiments gave conversion near 0.78–0.96. However, the campaign does not establish whether temperature, time, solvent, or catalyst was primarily responsible for that contrast.

Batch 5 is the cleanest evidence that 430 K for 7200 s did not catastrophically degrade the C1/S1 reaction mixture: its direct final assay gave recovery 0.292, purity 0.388, and degradation warning 0.0260, close to its preceding HPLC estimates of recovery 0.303 and purity 0.394. Nevertheless, longer or hotter operation could eventually favor D, and no safe optimum beyond the tested range should be inferred.

## 3. Extraction model and its failure to transfer cleanly

The material dossier suggested equilibrium partitioning of each solute j according to an effective distribution coefficient Kj. A conventional model would be:

fj,organic = Kj Vo/(Va + Kj Vo)

where Vo and Va are organic and aqueous volumes. The dossier’s X0 anchors reported a product organic fraction of 0.631 and an impurity organic fraction of 0.345 at its reference contact condition, with nominal selectivity ratio S* = 3.93. This made X0 a reasonable prior choice.

The actual reaction mixtures did not show the expected enrichment reliably. In batch 9, the pre-extraction HPLC purity was 0.608 and recovery was 0.485, but after X0 extraction and retention of the organic phase, the final assay gave purity 0.592 and recovery 0.235. The loss in recovery is qualitatively consistent with incomplete partitioning and phase rejection, but the absence of purity improvement contradicts a simple two-solute P/I partition model.

Plausible explanations include:

1. The dossier impurity anchor represents only one impurity, whereas the reaction generated several impurity or degradation classes with different partition coefficients.
2. The reaction solvent contributed to the effective phase composition, so the dossier’s nominal Va and Vo were not the actual thermodynamic phase volumes.
3. Catalyst, residual reagent, or emulsified material contributed to final-assay impurity.
4. The dossier may have been misindexed, as explicitly allowed by its public interpretation.
5. Extraction may not have reached the assumed equilibrium despite the nominal 240 s mixing and 180 s settling.

These alternatives cannot be distinguished from the available measurements because individual species concentrations and phase-specific mass balances were hidden.

## 4. Washing and downstream losses

Washing the retained organic phase was detrimental in the closest comparison available.

Batch 9 used C1/S2, X0 extraction, and no wash. It gave final purity 0.592 and recovery 0.235. Batch 11 used the same nominal reaction and extraction but applied two 0.01 L washes. Its reaction-stage HPLC result was similar—purity 0.599 and recovery 0.467 versus 0.608 and 0.485 in batch 9—yet its final purity fell to 0.510 and recovery to 0.132.

Because both purity and recovery declined by amounts much larger than the declared final-assay noise scales, the washes likely removed target preferentially, introduced or retained additional measured solute, or altered the selected-phase composition adversely. The result rejects the conjecture that repeated washing would raise purity for this particular process. It does not prove that all wash volumes or wash media are harmful.

Batch 2 used one wash after X0 extraction. Its final purity was 0.698 and recovery 0.0210, compared with reaction-stage purity 0.553 and recovery 0.106. This could indicate purification at substantial product loss, but it is not a matched unwashed comparison. The batch 9/11 comparison is therefore more persuasive for the tested C1/S2 process.

Batch 1 included washing, drying, and a 300 s concentration step. Its final assay reported purity 0.816 but recovery 0, selectivity 0.0140, and yield 0.00996. I do not interpret this as a successful high-purity isolation. It is more consistent with near-total target depletion followed by a ratio-based purity estimate on a very small remaining solute pool. Drying or concentration may have caused additional target loss, but their separate effects are unidentifiable because they were not isolated experimentally.

## 5. Why final conversion often approached one

After phase separation, batches 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10 often showed final-assay conversion near 0.99–1.00 even when their earlier reaction-stage HPLC conversion was much lower. For example, batch 2 changed from HPLC conversion 0.279 to final conversion 1.00.

This should not be read as continued chemical reaction to completion. The instrument contract states that downstream metrics apply to the selected phase and do not relabel an earlier reaction measurement. If unreacted R partitions mainly into the rejected aqueous or reactor phase, the retained organic phase can contain almost no R and therefore appear fully converted. Thus:

reaction conversion = reactor-wide chemical progress before workup
final selected-phase conversion = absence of reactant in the retained material

This scope distinction is essential. Final recovery and purity, rather than final conversion, are the relevant downstream performance measures.

## 6. Added component and atmosphere/control observations

Batch 4 added 0.04 mol of component 0 in addition to 0.04 mol reagent and used C3/S0 at 380 K for 3600 s. It gave HPLC conversion 0.201, purity 0.432, and recovery 0.0885; final purity was 0.594 and recovery 0.0205. Because catalyst identity also differed from the strongest catalyst and there was no matched no-component C3/S0 experiment, the role of component 0 is unidentifiable. It could be a second reactant, excess substrate, or an alternative charge representation. Its addition consumed the same limited reagent stock in the campaign ledger, so it should not be assumed to be a free additive.

Batch 12 attempted configured nitrogen control but became a procedural failure rather than a valid atmosphere comparison. The early HPLC observation after effectively negligible reaction time showed zero conversion and recovery. Subsequent prolonged controlled operation left no assayable material; terminate repeatedly returned `has_material=false`, and the batch was discarded. It supplies no valid evidence that nitrogen is favorable or unfavorable. Plausible causes include excessive cumulative controlled heating, controller-stage misuse, or complete destruction/depletion of the assayable solute pool.

## 7. Overall process interpretation

The dominant determinants of useful target formation were the joint catalyst/solvent choice and reaction severity. Among tested combinations, C1/S2 at 430 K for 7200 s was the strongest reaction recipe. Its best observed pre-workup result in batch 9 was approximately:

conversion 0.959
purity 0.608
recovery 0.485
selectivity 0.478

The extraction train then imposed a substantial recovery penalty without reliably improving purity. X0 extraction reduced batch 9 recovery to 0.235 and left purity at 0.592. Repeated washing reduced both further. Consequently, the tested world does not behave like a simple reaction followed by ideal selective partitioning; reaction impurities and downstream phase behavior are coupled.

A useful conceptual process equation is:

final recovery = reaction target yield × extraction retention × wash retention × transfer retention × survival during drying/concentration

final purity depends on the corresponding retention factors for every impurity, not only on target recovery. Batch 9 indicates a reaction target recovery around 0.485 and a net downstream target retention of roughly 0.235/0.485 ≈ 0.49. This ratio is only a descriptive estimate because the HPLC and final assay are independent noisy measurements and sample different material scopes.

## 8. Scope and unresolved alternatives

The following factors remain unidentifiable:

- Individual rate constants and activation energies.
- Whether solvent-S2 improves target formation kinetically, suppresses degradation, or changes analytical response.
- The number and identities of impurity classes.
- Individual phase partition coefficients for actual reaction impurities.
- Whether extraction reached equilibrium.
- Separate effects of drying and concentration.
- Atmosphere effects, because batch 12 was invalid as a controlled comparison.
- Reproducibility beyond the approximate batch 9/11 nominal repeat.

A plausible alternative model is that the measured “target” and “impurity” signals are not single species but reporter-weighted pools. In that case, catalyst and solvent could change response composition as well as chemical composition. Another alternative is kinetic phase transfer: product or impurity may continue transforming during mixing and settling, violating the assumption that workup is purely distributive.

## 9. Conclusion

The best-supported explanation is a network of competing target and impurity reactions whose relative rates depend strongly on catalyst–solvent pairing, followed by nonideal, multicomponent phase partitioning. C1/S2 at 430 K for 7200 s maximized observed reaction-stage recovery, but the tested extraction and wash operations could not deliver purity ≥0.80 while retaining meaningful target. Batch 1 was the sole completed batch whose final assay numerically crossed the purity threshold, at 0.816, but its recovery was reported as zero; it is therefore formally feasible under the strict threshold but not evidence of a practically successful isolation. The campaign identified a strong reaction condition and several harmful downstream operations, but it did not identify a satisfactory complete recovery–purity compromise.

payload.rationale: I treated catalyst loading relative to the reagent charge as a major extrapolation variable. Q01–Q06 use only 0.00025 mol catalyst with 0.04 mol reagent, one twentieth of the catalyst amount used in the closest campaign C1/S2 batches. A roughly catalyst-dependent effective rate therefore predicts little target formation at 400 K, especially after only 1800 s in Q01. The longer 7200 s recipes improve recovery, but washing, 600 s concentration, and the 0.97 transfer further reduce the small target pool. X0 is predicted to retain and discriminate target somewhat better than X2 (Q03 versus Q04); with X2, a smaller organic phase raises purity but lowers recovery (Q05), while a larger organic phase does the reverse (Q06). Q07–Q12 use 0.002 mol reagent, making the catalyst/reagent ratio comparable to campaign batches 9 and 11, so their fractional reaction recovery should be much higher. I anchored these estimates to batch 9 (C1/S2 reaction-stage purity 0.608 and recovery 0.485; unwashed X0 final purity 0.592 and recovery 0.235) and batch 11 (similar reaction stage, but two washes gave purity 0.510 and recovery 0.132). Accordingly, washing is predicted to reduce recovery and, based on the campaign rather than ideal partition theory, slightly reduce purity. Two staged washes in Q10 are assigned more loss than one wash of equal total volume in Q09. Concentration is also treated as a target-loss/degradation risk, so Q12 is lower than otherwise matched Q11. Intervals are deliberately broad because no campaign batch used the exact catalyst amount, 400 K condition, X2 workup, or isolated concentration comparison; near-zero recoveries in Q01–Q06 also make ratio-based purity particularly uncertain.

payload.report:
1. **Claims and laws**

No explicit instance-level mechanism or optimum prior was supplied. The material dossier supplied only scoped partition anchors and warned that they might be incomplete or misindexed.

- **Supported:** Catalyst and solvent jointly control competing target and impurity formation. Under otherwise similar 430 K/7200 s conditions in solvent S1, C1 in batch 5 outperformed C0, C2, and C3 in batches 6–8. Changing C1 from S1 to S2 improved reaction-stage purity and recovery from 0.394/0.303 in batch 5 to 0.608/0.485 in batch 9. This evidence changed my view from a generic temperature-dominated model to a catalyst–solvent selectivity model.
- **Partially supported:** Greater reaction severity increases conversion. The low-severity batches 1 and 2 had conversions of 0.098 and 0.279, while several 430 K/7200 s batches reached 0.78–0.96. Because catalyst and solvent also changed, a quantitative time or Arrhenius law remains untested.
- **Contradicted in this process:** The dossier-based expectation that X0 extraction would reliably enrich target. Batch 9 had reaction-stage purity 0.608 but final purity 0.592 after X0 extraction. This caused me to replace a two-solute equilibrium explanation with a multicomponent/nonideal workup explanation.
- **Contradicted:** The expectation that aqueous washing would improve purity. Nominally matched batches 9 and 11 began with similar HPLC results, but two washes in batch 11 reduced final purity and recovery to 0.510 and 0.132, versus 0.592 and 0.235 without washing in batch 9.
- **Untested or unresolved:** Individual kinetic constants, activation energies, true atmosphere effects, separate drying and concentration effects, and the roles of X1–X3 in actual reaction mixtures. Batch 12 was a procedural failure, not a valid nitrogen comparison. Batch 4 did not identify the role of component 0 because catalyst and other conditions were confounded.

2. **One discriminating experiment**

I would repeat the C1/S2 reaction from batch 9, then perform one X0 extraction at the dossier contact condition without washing, drying, or concentration. I would measure the reactor mixture immediately before extraction and assay both separated phases quantitatively, preserving a phase-resolved mass balance.

The leading explanation predicts that target mass should largely be accounted for across the two phases, but the observed target/impurity partition selectivity will be substantially poorer than the dossier anchor because the reaction contains additional impurity classes. If instead the two phases reproduce the dossier-like selectivity while total target mass is conserved, I would attribute the campaign’s poor finals mainly to washing, transfer, or later processing. A large mass-balance deficit immediately after extraction would favor physical loss, emulsion/non-equilibrium behavior, or continuing chemistry. Strong dependence on longer settling or repeated contact would weaken the equilibrium-partition model.

3. **Unused evidence, reliability, and goal effects**

Raw spectra and characterization artifacts were not inspected, and most byproduct, degradation-warning, and mass-balance channels were used only qualitatively. Cost and accumulated risk were not used to fit the mechanism. X1–X3 dossier properties were not experimentally validated, and no proper replicate series quantified process variability.

The sealed predictions are least reliable for Q01–Q06 because they extrapolate to a twenty-fold lower catalyst amount and to X2 workups absent from the campaign. Q09–Q10 are also weak because wash staging was never isolated, while Q11–Q12 extrapolate an unisolated concentration effect. Predictions for the 0.002 mol charge are uncertain because campaign reactions mostly used 0.04 mol. The batch 1 recommendation is particularly fragile: it was selected only because its measured purity of 0.816 met the formal threshold, while recovery was zero and washing, drying, and concentration were confounded.

The purity constraint affected evidence collection. It encouraged additional extraction and washing trials and forced selection of batch 1 despite negligible recovery. More balanced research would have reserved batches for matched reaction replicates, phase-resolved mass balances, and isolated downstream-operation comparisons. The main conflict was therefore between satisfying the strict feasibility rule and learning a robust high-recovery process.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 1 is the only completed batch whose final assay met the mandatory purity threshold (purity 0.8165). Its recovery was reported as zero, so the campaign did not identify a satisfactory feasible recovery–purity compromise; nevertheless, under the strict constraint it is preferable to higher-recovery batches 9 and 11, whose final purities (0.5922 and 0.5104) were infeasible.
